notes.text: Sorrow — The prophet now seems to speak, how greatly the calamity of this people affected him.
Why — As if God should seem to reply; let them not think it strange, seeing they have turned their backs upon me, and trusted to idols.

Am I hurt — The prophet here shews how deeply he is affected with the peoples misery. Black - I am as those that are clad in deep mourning. The prophet's lamentation continues over their adultery, deceit, idolatry, which God would certainly punish, and they should be laid waste, when they should sufficiently lament, ver. 1-22. No trust in ourselves, but in God, who will punish all nations, ver. 23- 26.

glossa.text: *My sorrow. ((ID.))* These things are to be read in the person of the Lord, bewailing the overthrow of Jerusalem, and not bearing her misery.

*And behold the voice.* He describes the weeping and the howling of the city when the enemies have entered in. The enemies coming from a far land cry out against the city, or the citizens against the enemies.
*The harvest is past.* The words of the people shut up in Jerusalem by the long siege, because changed are the times, the circuit of the year rolled round. But our hope is void.
*For the breach.* The Lord's answer, who in the affliction of Jerusalem is seen to be afflicted.

*Who will give. ((HIER.))* The king of Jerusalem, the city being besieged by the enemies, etc., *as far as* but this can be understood as well in the person of the Lord as in the person of the prophet.

notes.text: Prevent — Prevent our utter extirpation.

glossa.text:
*A psalm of Asaph.* ((CASS.)) The second psalm of lamentation. He prays Christ to come to the help of the nation which for its hardness is to be grievously afflicted. We are admonished to rejoice at the good things of our neighbours, and to be afflicted at their calamities.

*O God, the nations are come.* ((ID.)) The first thing is the complaint, and there are numbered how great things Jerusalem bore in the times of Antiochus, when it was not destroyed, and by these the persecution of the Church is signified. ((AUG.)) *They are come.* He does not speak as to one that knows not, etc., *as far as* but now they are plainly fulfilled.

*Into thy inheritance.* ((ID.)) Of the people of Israel; the inheritance of God are the elect, but not the blinded; therefore these things can be said of the times after the ascension of Christ; but also before Christ had come, for then too there was an inheritance, where the Prophets were, and the saints led away into Babylon; or most of all under Antiochus. ((CASS.)) But if any man, etc., *as far as* whose circuit is through the whole world, where the persecution also is.

*The dead bodies.* ((CASS.)) Carcases, as though they raged not only against the living. To bury belongs to piety, to cast forth belongs to cruelty. *They have poured out.* ((ID.)) He heightens it, that he may move the judge.

*We are become.* ((CASS.)) The glory of Jerusalem, wonderful in the whole world, is turned into *a reproach to our neighbours,* which is heavier than if it were to men far off, because these are always at hand. Or, the neighbours are the affections, the kinsfolk being now willing to believe, so that the martyrs say this.

*How long, O Lord?* ((CASS.)) A prayer on his own behalf against enemies and insulting neighbours; as though they rage thus: But, O Lord, how long? ((AUG.)) He asks that he be not angry unto the end, that is, that that laying waste may not continue, but that he temper his correction. By the name of *wrath* is understood the vengeance upon iniquity, by the name of *jealousy,* the exacting of chastity, that the soul may not commit fornication away from God. Note that this befalls men for their sins, though they be just, as the three children and the Prophets in the captivity bear witness. *As fire.* ((ID.)) Burn so long, until the gold of the virtues be perfectly purged, and the wood, that is the vices, be turned to ashes.

*They have devoured.* ((AUG.)) By delivering them to the teeth of wild beasts. *They have laid waste,* by the overthrow of the city, which was stripped of its own citizens, or because they slew those put in the place of the citizens who had been slain; Jacob for the man, the man, that is, for the nation which offended. The patriarch is pleasing, that the memory of him may soften the sins of the people. *Jacob.* ((AUG.)) This is the inheritance spoken of above. *The place.* ((CASS.)) The city, where the temple was, to which they were gathered for the feasts.

*Of our iniquities.* ((BEDA.)) That is, those which we have contracted from our fathers, to whom, that is to say, correction is no longer owed, but damnation, unless the compassion of thy grace be at hand. For it is written: *The soul that shall sin, the same shall die.* And, *I will visit the sins of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation ((Ezech. XVIII.)) Of old.* (CASS.) He does not speak of past ones only, since in this time also certain Jews were following idols; but of the like of the ancient ones, in which they sinned through countless years. *Let them prevent us.* ((ID.)) Before the judgment which every man fears, because unless indulgence go before in the judgment, the guilty man is not acquitted. *Exceedingly.* Lest any man presume upon his deeds.

*Help us.* ((CASS.)) In the war for the defence of the laws, because they trust not in their own powers, but in the powers of God. *For the glory.* Not for our merit; that, being delivered, we may render honour to thy name. *For the glory of thy name.* Let it be ascribed to the goodness of the holy name, not to us, since it cannot be had by our own deeds. *Help us, O God.* By this he is neither ungrateful to grace, nor does he take away free choice. For he who is helped does something also through himself. *Deliver us.* ((AUG.)) He delivers, that is, he rescues from evils, since he both helps us to do righteousness, and is propitious to the sins without which there is no living here.

notes.text:
I exhort therefore — Seeing God is so gracious. In this chapter he gives directions,

1. With regard to public prayers

2. With regard to doctrine. Supplication is here the imploring help in time of need: prayer is any kind of offering up our desires to God. But true prayer is the vehemency of holy zeal, the ardour of divine love, arising from a calm, undisturbed soul, moved upon by the Spirit of God. Intercession is prayer for others. We may likewise give thanks for all men, in the full sense of the word, for that God "willeth all men to be saved," and Christ is the Mediator of all.

For all that are in authority — Seeing even the lowest country magistrates frequently do much good or much harm. God supports the power of magistracy for the sake of his own people, when, in the present state of men, it could not otherwise be kept up in any nation whatever. Godliness - Inward religion; the true worship of God. Honesty - A comprehensive word taking in the whole duty we owe to our neighbour.

For this — That we pray for all men. Do you ask, "Why are not more converted?" We do not pray enough. Is acceptable in the sight of God our saviour - Who has actually saved us that believe, and willeth all men to be saved. It is strange that any whom he has actually saved should doubt the universality of his grace!

Who willeth seriously all men — Not a part only, much less the smallest part. To be saved - Eternally. This is treated of, ver. 5, 6. And, in order thereto, to come - They are not compelled. To the knowledge of the truth - Which brings salvation. This is treated of, ver. 6, 7.

For — The fourth verse is proved by the fifth; the first, by the fourth. There is one God - And they who have not him, through the one Mediator, have no God. One mediator also - We could not rejoice that there is a God, were there not a mediator also; one who stands between God and men, to reconcile man to God, and to transact the whole affair of our salvation. This excludes all other mediators, as saints and angels, whom the Papists set up and idolatrously worship as such: just as the heathens of old set up many mediators, to pacify their superior gods. The man - Therefore all men are to apply to this mediator, "who gave himself for all."

Who gave himself a ransom for all — Such a ransom, the word signifies, wherein a like or equal is given; as an eye for an eye, or life for life: and this ransom, from the dignity of the person redeeming, was more than equivalent to all mankind. To be testified of in due season - Literally, in his own seasons; those chosen by his own wisdom.

glossa.text: *I beseech.* Hitherto concerning the false apostles, here concerning prayers. *First of all.* That is, that supplications be made before all things. Here the order of the Mass is shown, which is a special kind of prayer. *Supplications.* Or that prayer which is made beside or before the consecration. *Prayers.* That is, in the consecration itself. *Petitions.* Or interpellations, as it were of debt, that what is here transacted may be perfected in eternal life, as when the people is blessed by the bishop. *Thanksgivings.* Concerning things done, which conclude the whole as though the whole were from God: as, Let us bless the Lord. *For all.* That we may follow the clemency of God, because God wills all men to be saved, although according to justice he reprobates certain ones. *That quiet* from persecution.

*For this.* Lest anyone should think that these things are not to be done for those whom the Church suffers, he adds: *For this is good.* And lest anyone should think that salvation could be had by the worship of the one God and by a good life without participation in the body of Christ, that is, without the faith of the Church. *One,* he says, *God, and one mediator,* that all men be saved may never come to pass save through the mediator, God the Word, which always was, yet according to the flesh was made.

*The mediator of God,* etc. This is that arbiter whom Job desires, saying: *Would that there were an arbiter for us.* 

((AUG., lib. IX de Civit. Dei, c. 15.)) A mediator between God and men, it behoved that he should have something like to God, etc., *as far as* another good one, who reconciles enemies, Jesus Christ.

*And in truth* Truth to come is the reality and the reward of faith. Dost thou ask, the reward? let faith go before. For we believe that we may know, we do not know that we may believe. For what is faith, save to believe what thou seest not? faith therefore is, to believe what thou seest not. Truth, to see what thou hast believed.

notes.text: To beg I am ashamed — But not ashamed to cheat! This was likewise a sense of honour! "By men called honour, but by angels pride."
I know — That is, I am resolved, what to do.

And the Lord commended the unjust steward — Namely, in this respect, because he had used timely precaution: so that though the dishonesty of such a servant be detestable, yet his foresight, care, and contrivance, about the interests of this life, deserve our imitation, with regard to the more important affairs of another. The children of this world - Those who seek no other portion than this world: Are wiser - Not absolutely, for they are, one and all, egregious fools; but they are more consistent with themselves; they are truer to their principles; they more steadily pursue their end; they are wiser in their generation - That is, in their own way, than the children of light - The children of God, whose light shines on their hearts.

And I say to you — Be good stewards even of the lowest talents wherewith God hath intrusted you. Mammon means riches or money. It is termed the mammon of unrighteousness, because of the manner wherein it is commonly either procured or employed. Make yourselves friends of this, by doing all possible good, particularly to the children of God: that when ye fail, when your flesh and your heart faileth, when this earthly tabernacle is dissolved, those of them who have gone before may receive, may welcome you into the everlasting habitations.

And whether ye have more or less, see that ye be faithful as well as wise stewards. He that is faithful in what is meanest of all, worldly substance, is also faithful in things of a higher nature; and he that uses these lowest gifts unfaithfully, is likewise unfaithful in spiritual things.
Who will intrust you with the true riches? — How should God intrust you with spiritual and eternal, which alone are true riches?

If ye have not been faithful in that which was another's — None of these temporal things are yours: you are only stewards of them, not proprietors: God is the proprietor of all; he lodges them in your hands for a season: but still they are his property. Rich men, understand and consider this. If your steward uses any part of your estate (so called in the language of men) any farther or any otherwise than you direct, he is a knave: he has neither conscience nor honour. Neither have you either one or the other, if you use any part of that estate, which is in truth God's, not yours, any otherwise than he directs. That which is your own - Heaven, which when you have it, will be your own forever.
And you cannot be faithful to God, if you trim between God and the world, if you do not serve him alone. Matt. vi, 24.

glossa.text: *To the disciples.* Because the Pharisees, being proud and avaricious, just as they denied pardon to those who asked it, so denied money to those in need; therefore the Saviour now speaks to them, now in their hearing speaks to the disciples, concerning mercy. *A certain man.* A bailiff, properly, is the keeper of a farm, but the word is put here for a steward, that is, a dispenser, who dispenses the whole substance of the house. For in this dispenser we ought not to take all things for imitation, namely that we should act fraudulently toward God. But on the contrary these similitudes are given, that we may understand that if he who wrought fraud could be praised by his lord, how much more does he please God who does those works according to his precept.

*A hundred cadi.* A cadus in Greek is called in Latin an amphora, holding three urns. A chorus is filled with thirty pecks. It can simply be taken thus: whoever relieves the need of a poor man, whether by a half or by a fifth part, is to be endowed with the wages of his own mercy.

*And the Lord commended.* If the dispenser of the unjust mammon is praised by the Lord's own voice because out of an unjust thing he made ready righteousness for himself, and, though he suffered loss, yet he praises his prudence, not because he had acted fraudulently against his lord, but because he had acted prudently for himself: how much more shall Christ, who can sustain no loss and is inclined to clemency, praise the disciples, if they have been merciful toward those entrusted to them. *The children of this world.* Whose works a man does, his son also he is called; whence: *The children of this world,* that is, of darkness; and the children of light, of eternal life.

*Make unto you.* Mammon, in the tongue of the Syrians, is the riches of iniquity, because they were gathered out of iniquity. If therefore iniquity well dispensed is turned into righteousness, how much more do the feasts of the divine word, in which there is no iniquity, lift up a good dispenser into heaven.

*He that is faithful.* In money that is to be shared with the poor man. *And in that which is greater.* Cleaving to the Creator, and made one spirit with him. But he who does not well dispense the temporal things he possesses, empties out for himself the glory of eternal things, over which he swells.

*If therefore,* etc. He who does not give to his brethren for their use what was created by God for all, will be unjust in dividing spiritual money, so that he divides the Lord's teaching not according to need, but according to persons.
*And if in that which is another's.* If you do not well dispense the carnal riches which slip away, who will give you the true and eternal riches?

*No servant.* Rebuking avarice, he says that the lovers of money are not able God with love; he therefore who loves God despises money: for it avails not to love things transitory and things eternal at once.

*Or he will hold to the one. ((AUG.))* He will not indeed love. For no man loves, etc., *as far as* and he flatters himself concerning his goodness and his impunity.

*You cannot,* etc. He does not say to have riches, but to serve them. He serves who guards them as a servant; but he who has shaken off the yoke of servitude distributes as a lord. He who serves mammon assuredly serves him who, being set over these things by the desert of his own perversity, is called by the Lord the prince of the world.

echoes.text: Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to Yahweh for it; for in its peace you shall have peace.
echoes.note: Paul's directive to pray for kings and all in high places that believers may lead a tranquil life echoes Jeremiah's letter urging the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon and pray to the LORD for it, because in its peace they will find peace. Both texts ground intercession for pagan rulers in the community's own well-being under foreign power. The logic of praying for the governing authority's order so that God's people may flourish is structurally identical.

echoes.text: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked? says the Lord Yahweh; and not rather that he should return from his way, and live?
echoes.note: God's declared desire that all be saved and come to knowledge of the truth echoes the LORD's protest that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but desires that they turn and live. Both passages assert a universal divine will for life and salvation rather than condemnation. Verse 32 of the same chapter reinforces this with the appeal to turn and live.

echoes.text: “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.
echoes.note: The call 'Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth, for I am God and there is no other' fuses the universal saving will with strict monotheism, precisely the pairing Paul makes in 'who desires all to be saved' and 'there is one God.' Isaiah's universal salvation offer grounded in the oneness of God stands directly behind this passage. The verbal and theological overlap is strong.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.
echoes.note: 'There is one God' restates the Shema's confession that the LORD is one, the foundational monotheistic creed of Israel. Paul reframes the Shema christologically by adding the one mediator, but the bedrock affirmation of divine oneness is directly drawn from Deuteronomy. This is the clearest scriptural anchor of verse 5.

echoes.text: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand. After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall […]
echoes.note: The Servant who makes his life an offering for sin and bears the sin of many provides the scriptural template for Christ giving himself as a ransom for all. The substitutionary self-offering 'for many' is universalized by Paul to 'for all.' The Servant Song is a primary source for the ransom theology of verse 6.

echoes.text: that they may offer sacrifices of pleasant aroma to the God of heaven, and pray for the life of the king, and of his sons.
echoes.note: The Persian decree provides for sacrifices and prayers 'for the life of the king and his sons,' a precedent for the synagogue practice of intercession for the ruling power that Paul commends to the church. This institutionalized prayer for the Gentile monarch stands behind the apostolic instruction. The continuity of Jewish intercession for kings informs the exhortation.

echoes.text: and pray for the life of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon, and for the life of Baltasar his son, that their days may be as the days of heaven above the earth: and the Lord will give us strength, and lighten our eyes, and we shall live under the shadow of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon, and under the shadow of Baltasar his son, and we shall serve them many days, and find favor in their sight.
echoes.note: Baruch directs prayer for the life of Nebuchadnezzar and his son Belshazzar, that the exiles may live under their shadow and find favor, mirroring the petition for kings so believers can live quietly. The deuterocanonical text models the very practice of interceding for a foreign sovereign's reign for the sake of the people's peace. It is a close conceptual parallel to verses 1-2.

echoes.text: Tell them, As I live, says the Lord Yahweh, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn, turn from your evil ways; for why will you die, house of Israel?
echoes.note: The oath 'As I live, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live' restates the divine saving desire that Paul invokes in saying God wills all people to be saved. The emphatic divine self-witness to a will for repentance and life parallels Paul's theology of God our Savior. It complements the Ezekiel 18 echo.

echoes.text: There is no umpire between us, that might lay his hand on us both.
echoes.note: Job's lament that 'there is no umpire between us, who might lay his hand on us both' articulates the need for a mediator between God and man that Paul declares fulfilled in the one mediator Christ Jesus. The longing for an arbitrator standing between God and humanity is answered in verse 5. The conceptual correspondence to 'one mediator' is notable though not verbal quotation.

echoes.text: On the next day, Moses said to the people, “You have sinned a great sin. Now I will go up to Yahweh. Perhaps I shall make atonement for your sin.” Moses returned to Yahweh, and said, “Oh, this people have sinned a great sin, and have made themselves gods of gold. Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.”
echoes.note: Moses standing between the LORD and the people, offering himself to make atonement for their sin, typifies the role of the one mediator that Paul ascribes to Christ. The Mosaic mediation at Sinai is the paradigmatic Old Testament instance of a man interceding between God and men. Christ as mediator is read against this figural background.

echoes.text: “When you take a census of the children of Israel, according to those who are numbered among them, then each man shall give a ransom for his soul to Yahweh, when you number them; that there be no plague among them when you number them.
echoes.note: The atonement money, a ransom for each life given at the census so that no plague befall them, supplies the cultic background for Christ giving himself as 'a ransom for all.' The Hebrew kopher / lytron concept of a redemptive price for life stands behind Paul's ransom language. The universalizing 'for all' extends the Exodus ransom to all humanity.

echoes.text: The king’s heart is in Yahweh’s hand like the watercourses. He turns it wherever he desires.
echoes.note: The conviction that the king's heart is a watercourse in the LORD's hand, turned wherever he wills, undergirds the rationale for praying for rulers: God can move them toward conditions of peace. Paul's confidence that prayer for kings yields a tranquil life presupposes divine sovereignty over rulers. The link is thematic rather than verbal and is faint.

echoes.text: Don’t we all have one father? Hasn’t one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, profaning the covenant of our fathers?
echoes.note: 'Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us?' offers a parallel monotheistic confession linked to the unity of humanity, resonant with Paul's 'one God' grounding the universality of salvation. The pairing of divine oneness with the common bond of all people overlaps with the passage. The connection is thematic and secondary to the Shema.

echoes.text: (I stood between Yahweh and you at that time, to show you Yahweh’s word: for you were afraid because of the fire, and didn’t go up onto the mountain;) saying,
echoes.note: Moses' statement that he stood between the LORD and the people to declare the word, because they feared the fire, presents him as mediator of the covenant, prefiguring the one mediator language. The Mosaic mediatorial office informs Paul's category. The link is figural and faint.

echoes.text: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough,
echoes.note: The psalm's note that no one can by any means ransom another or give to God a price for his life sets up, by contrast, the ransom that Christ alone provides 'for all.' Paul's ransom claim answers the human impossibility the psalm laments. The link is conceptual and contrastive.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest. How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you arise out of your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: so your poverty will come as a robber, and your scarcity as an armed man.
echoes.note: The manager's frantic foresight against future destitution ('I have no strength to dig, I am ashamed to beg') inverts the sluggard wisdom of Proverbs, where prudent provision against want is praised. The shared topos of provident foresight versus ruinous idleness gives modest coherence, though no verbal contact; faint and contested.

echoes.text: There was no bread in all the land; for the famine was very severe, so that the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan fainted by reason of the famine. Joseph gathered up all the money that was found in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, for the grain which they bought: and Joseph brought the money into Pharaoh’s house. When the money was all spent in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph, and said, “Give […]
echoes.note: Joseph as the shrewd steward managing his lord's grain and debtors during scarcity offers a figural backdrop to a manager renegotiating debts of wheat and oil. Coherence is thematic (estate-steward over produce), but the moral valence is opposite and there is no diction overlap, so it is faint and contested.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Make friends by means of unrighteous mammon, so that they may receive you into the eternal tents' coheres tightly with the proverb that lending to the poor lends to the LORD, who repays. The shared logic that present generosity with money secures future, divine reception gives strong coherence with a widely available sapiential maxim.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's counsel that almsgiving 'lays up a good treasure against the day of necessity' and 'delivers from death' supplies the precise economy Jesus assumes: wealth converted into mercy yields eschatological security. High coherence and Second-Temple availability make this a strong deuterocanonical echo behind 'receive you into the eternal tents.'

echoes.text: Howbeit with a man in poor estate be longsuffering; And let him not wait for your alms. Help a poor man for the commandment’s sake; And according to his need send him not empty away. Lose your money for a brother and a friend; And let it not rust under the stone to be lost. Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold. Shut up alms in your store-chambers; And it shall deliver you out of all […]
echoes.note: Ben Sira urges laying up alms in one's treasury as a deposit that will rescue one from misfortune, framing charity to the poor as deferred self-interest. The volume and coherence with 'make friends... so they may receive you' is high, and Sirach was demonstrably available to Luke's milieu.

echoes.text: Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor; if there may be a lengthening of your tranquility.
echoes.note: Daniel's appeal to Nebuchadnezzar to 'redeem your sins by almsgiving and your iniquities by mercy to the poor' supplies the redemptive-almsgiving theology underlying using mammon to gain eternal welcome. Strong coherence with the verse's logic; the connection is conceptual rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Incline your ear to a poor man, And answer him with peaceful words in meekness. Deliver him that is wronged from the hand of him that wrongeth him; And be not faint-hearted in giving judgement. Be as a father to the fatherless, And instead of a husband to their mother: So will you be as a son of the Most High, And he will love you more than your mother does.
echoes.note: The maxim 'faithful in a very little is faithful in much' coheres with Ben Sira's wisdom that integrity in small dealings with the lowly proves character, but the gnomic form is broadly diffused and no single passage controls it. Faint and contested as a specific source.

echoes.text: If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose this day whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.”
echoes.note: 'No servant can serve two masters... you cannot serve God and Mammon' echoes the covenantal either/or of choosing whom to serve, the LORD versus rival gods. Coherence with the exclusive-service motif is real but the diction is independent, so it is a faint figural echo at best.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The demand for undivided love of God set against love of money draws on the Shema's totalizing claim ('with all your heart'), which forbids a divided heart. The opposition of single-hearted devotion versus a rival master gives modest coherence; verbal contact is absent, so it is contested.

doctrine.article: Art. XX, the One Oblation of Christ

notes.text: To fail — Either to root them out, or to enslave them.

When — Ye that could wish there were nothing to interrupt your marketing, that look on solemn times of worship as burdensome, such was the first day of every month, and the weekly sabbath. Small - So the ephah being too little, the poor buyer had not his due. The shekel great - They weighed the money which they received, and had no more justice, than to make their shekel weight greater than the standard; so the poor were twice oppressed, had less than was their right, and paid more than they ought to pay.

That we may buy — They would have new moons and sabbaths over, that they might go to market to buy the poor. And when these poor owed but for a very little commodity, as suppose a pair of shoes, these merciless men would take the advantage against them, and make them sell themselves to pay the debt. The refuse - This was another kind of oppression, corrupted wares, sold to those that were necessitous.
Hath sworn — By himself. Forget - Suffer to pass unpunished.
Humbleth — Who is so high, that it is a wonderful condescention in him to take any notice of his heavenly host, and much more of sinful and miserable men upon earth.

Princes — As he did Joseph, David, and others. His people - Who in God's account are far more honourable than the princes of Heathen nations. This and the four following psalms, the Jews were wont to sing at the close of the paschal supper. It is a solemn commemoration of God's delivering Israel, giving them the law, and water out of the rock, ver. 1-8.

glossa.text: *Praise ye.* ((ID.)) First the Prophet admonishes the devout to praise continually, and everywhere to preach. Secondly he himself does what he admonishes others to do, that is, he praises God there: *Who is as the Lord ((I Cor. XIV))*? Admonishing therefore unto praise, he shows and says who and whom, and how long, and where, and why they should praise. *Children.* Not in sense, but in malice, and chiefly in pride, that is, the humble; whence, *Be not children in sense, but in malice be children, that in mind ye may be perfect.* ((AUG., CASS.)) Praise the Lord, ye children, the simple and the pure, who ought to praise.

*Let the name be.* ((CASS.)) Behold, he has said who and whom they ought to praise; then he subjoins how long we praise *laudamus*; read *laudandus*, "is to be praised", namely always. *Let the name of the Lord be:* lest ye think that I command praise for an hour, etc., *as far as* by the Gentiles the carnal, by the heavens the spiritual.
*From the rising of the sun.* ((AUG.)) Here he says that he ought to be praised everywhere.
*Above the heavens.* ((ID.)) The Apostles, through whom he reigns among the Gentiles, and is; therefore I invite to praises, because he is to reign above all.

*Who is as.* ((CASS.)) Secondly he himself does what he admonishes others to do, that by the deed also he may teach others. *Who?* None that can of himself. *In the high places,* etc. In the angels and the saints: and although he is high, he despises not the lowly.

*The lowly things.* These are they who by his gift are made high, and in them he sits. *He beholdeth,* the lowly one by one. *In the earth,* the saints, whom he so beholds as, on the contrary, he hates the proud.
*Raising up from the earth:* from the labour of the body. *Out of the dunghill,* he is lifted up over whom the vices of the flesh have no dominion.

*Who maketh to dwell.* ((CASS., AUG.)) He expounds where he raises up and lifts up, etc., *as far as* out of the mammon of iniquity by works of mercy. *The barren woman.* ((AUG.)) Namely Sara, that is, the Gentile Church, which was barren before, whereby she is signified by Sara. Her, I say, he makes to dwell in the house, that is, in the Church of the Jews, among the Jews themselves, that in the corner-stone the two walls may be joined together, and there may be made one fold. *Of children.* ((ID.)) In whose person these things are said, etc., *as far as* since I know myself to be without children, and a widow.

notes.text:
I exhort therefore — Seeing God is so gracious. In this chapter he gives directions,

1. With regard to public prayers

2. With regard to doctrine. Supplication is here the imploring help in time of need: prayer is any kind of offering up our desires to God. But true prayer is the vehemency of holy zeal, the ardour of divine love, arising from a calm, undisturbed soul, moved upon by the Spirit of God. Intercession is prayer for others. We may likewise give thanks for all men, in the full sense of the word, for that God "willeth all men to be saved," and Christ is the Mediator of all.

For all that are in authority — Seeing even the lowest country magistrates frequently do much good or much harm. God supports the power of magistracy for the sake of his own people, when, in the present state of men, it could not otherwise be kept up in any nation whatever. Godliness - Inward religion; the true worship of God. Honesty - A comprehensive word taking in the whole duty we owe to our neighbour.

For this — That we pray for all men. Do you ask, "Why are not more converted?" We do not pray enough. Is acceptable in the sight of God our saviour - Who has actually saved us that believe, and willeth all men to be saved. It is strange that any whom he has actually saved should doubt the universality of his grace!

Who willeth seriously all men — Not a part only, much less the smallest part. To be saved - Eternally. This is treated of, ver. 5, 6. And, in order thereto, to come - They are not compelled. To the knowledge of the truth - Which brings salvation. This is treated of, ver. 6, 7.

For — The fourth verse is proved by the fifth; the first, by the fourth. There is one God - And they who have not him, through the one Mediator, have no God. One mediator also - We could not rejoice that there is a God, were there not a mediator also; one who stands between God and men, to reconcile man to God, and to transact the whole affair of our salvation. This excludes all other mediators, as saints and angels, whom the Papists set up and idolatrously worship as such: just as the heathens of old set up many mediators, to pacify their superior gods. The man - Therefore all men are to apply to this mediator, "who gave himself for all."

Who gave himself a ransom for all — Such a ransom, the word signifies, wherein a like or equal is given; as an eye for an eye, or life for life: and this ransom, from the dignity of the person redeeming, was more than equivalent to all mankind. To be testified of in due season - Literally, in his own seasons; those chosen by his own wisdom.

glossa.text: *I beseech.* Hitherto concerning the false apostles, here concerning prayers. *First of all.* That is, that supplications be made before all things. Here the order of the Mass is shown, which is a special kind of prayer. *Supplications.* Or that prayer which is made beside or before the consecration. *Prayers.* That is, in the consecration itself. *Petitions.* Or interpellations, as it were of debt, that what is here transacted may be perfected in eternal life, as when the people is blessed by the bishop. *Thanksgivings.* Concerning things done, which conclude the whole as though the whole were from God: as, Let us bless the Lord. *For all.* That we may follow the clemency of God, because God wills all men to be saved, although according to justice he reprobates certain ones. *That quiet* from persecution.

*For this.* Lest anyone should think that these things are not to be done for those whom the Church suffers, he adds: *For this is good.* And lest anyone should think that salvation could be had by the worship of the one God and by a good life without participation in the body of Christ, that is, without the faith of the Church. *One,* he says, *God, and one mediator,* that all men be saved may never come to pass save through the mediator, God the Word, which always was, yet according to the flesh was made.

*The mediator of God,* etc. This is that arbiter whom Job desires, saying: *Would that there were an arbiter for us.* 

((AUG., lib. IX de Civit. Dei, c. 15.)) A mediator between God and men, it behoved that he should have something like to God, etc., *as far as* another good one, who reconciles enemies, Jesus Christ.

*And in truth* Truth to come is the reality and the reward of faith. Dost thou ask, the reward? let faith go before. For we believe that we may know, we do not know that we may believe. For what is faith, save to believe what thou seest not? faith therefore is, to believe what thou seest not. Truth, to see what thou hast believed.

notes.text: To beg I am ashamed — But not ashamed to cheat! This was likewise a sense of honour! "By men called honour, but by angels pride."
I know — That is, I am resolved, what to do.

And the Lord commended the unjust steward — Namely, in this respect, because he had used timely precaution: so that though the dishonesty of such a servant be detestable, yet his foresight, care, and contrivance, about the interests of this life, deserve our imitation, with regard to the more important affairs of another. The children of this world - Those who seek no other portion than this world: Are wiser - Not absolutely, for they are, one and all, egregious fools; but they are more consistent with themselves; they are truer to their principles; they more steadily pursue their end; they are wiser in their generation - That is, in their own way, than the children of light - The children of God, whose light shines on their hearts.

And I say to you — Be good stewards even of the lowest talents wherewith God hath intrusted you. Mammon means riches or money. It is termed the mammon of unrighteousness, because of the manner wherein it is commonly either procured or employed. Make yourselves friends of this, by doing all possible good, particularly to the children of God: that when ye fail, when your flesh and your heart faileth, when this earthly tabernacle is dissolved, those of them who have gone before may receive, may welcome you into the everlasting habitations.

And whether ye have more or less, see that ye be faithful as well as wise stewards. He that is faithful in what is meanest of all, worldly substance, is also faithful in things of a higher nature; and he that uses these lowest gifts unfaithfully, is likewise unfaithful in spiritual things.
Who will intrust you with the true riches? — How should God intrust you with spiritual and eternal, which alone are true riches?

If ye have not been faithful in that which was another's — None of these temporal things are yours: you are only stewards of them, not proprietors: God is the proprietor of all; he lodges them in your hands for a season: but still they are his property. Rich men, understand and consider this. If your steward uses any part of your estate (so called in the language of men) any farther or any otherwise than you direct, he is a knave: he has neither conscience nor honour. Neither have you either one or the other, if you use any part of that estate, which is in truth God's, not yours, any otherwise than he directs. That which is your own - Heaven, which when you have it, will be your own forever.
And you cannot be faithful to God, if you trim between God and the world, if you do not serve him alone. Matt. vi, 24.

glossa.text: *To the disciples.* Because the Pharisees, being proud and avaricious, just as they denied pardon to those who asked it, so denied money to those in need; therefore the Saviour now speaks to them, now in their hearing speaks to the disciples, concerning mercy. *A certain man.* A bailiff, properly, is the keeper of a farm, but the word is put here for a steward, that is, a dispenser, who dispenses the whole substance of the house. For in this dispenser we ought not to take all things for imitation, namely that we should act fraudulently toward God. But on the contrary these similitudes are given, that we may understand that if he who wrought fraud could be praised by his lord, how much more does he please God who does those works according to his precept.

*A hundred cadi.* A cadus in Greek is called in Latin an amphora, holding three urns. A chorus is filled with thirty pecks. It can simply be taken thus: whoever relieves the need of a poor man, whether by a half or by a fifth part, is to be endowed with the wages of his own mercy.

*And the Lord commended.* If the dispenser of the unjust mammon is praised by the Lord's own voice because out of an unjust thing he made ready righteousness for himself, and, though he suffered loss, yet he praises his prudence, not because he had acted fraudulently against his lord, but because he had acted prudently for himself: how much more shall Christ, who can sustain no loss and is inclined to clemency, praise the disciples, if they have been merciful toward those entrusted to them. *The children of this world.* Whose works a man does, his son also he is called; whence: *The children of this world,* that is, of darkness; and the children of light, of eternal life.

*Make unto you.* Mammon, in the tongue of the Syrians, is the riches of iniquity, because they were gathered out of iniquity. If therefore iniquity well dispensed is turned into righteousness, how much more do the feasts of the divine word, in which there is no iniquity, lift up a good dispenser into heaven.

*He that is faithful.* In money that is to be shared with the poor man. *And in that which is greater.* Cleaving to the Creator, and made one spirit with him. But he who does not well dispense the temporal things he possesses, empties out for himself the glory of eternal things, over which he swells.

*If therefore,* etc. He who does not give to his brethren for their use what was created by God for all, will be unjust in dividing spiritual money, so that he divides the Lord's teaching not according to need, but according to persons.
*And if in that which is another's.* If you do not well dispense the carnal riches which slip away, who will give you the true and eternal riches?

*No servant.* Rebuking avarice, he says that the lovers of money are not able God with love; he therefore who loves God despises money: for it avails not to love things transitory and things eternal at once.

*Or he will hold to the one. ((AUG.))* He will not indeed love. For no man loves, etc., *as far as* and he flatters himself concerning his goodness and his impunity.

*You cannot,* etc. He does not say to have riches, but to serve them. He serves who guards them as a servant; but he who has shaken off the yoke of servitude distributes as a lord. He who serves mammon assuredly serves him who, being set over these things by the desert of his own perversity, is called by the Lord the prince of the world.

Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to Yahweh for it; for in its peace you shall have peace.
echoes.note: Paul's directive to pray for kings and all in high places that believers may lead a tranquil life echoes Jeremiah's letter urging the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon and pray to the LORD for it, because in its peace they will find peace. Both texts ground intercession for pagan rulers in the community's own well-being under foreign power. The logic of praying for the governing authority's order so that God's people may flourish is structurally identical.

echoes.text: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked? says the Lord Yahweh; and not rather that he should return from his way, and live?
echoes.note: God's declared desire that all be saved and come to knowledge of the truth echoes the LORD's protest that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but desires that they turn and live. Both passages assert a universal divine will for life and salvation rather than condemnation. Verse 32 of the same chapter reinforces this with the appeal to turn and live.

echoes.text: “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.
echoes.note: The call 'Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth, for I am God and there is no other' fuses the universal saving will with strict monotheism, precisely the pairing Paul makes in 'who desires all to be saved' and 'there is one God.' Isaiah's universal salvation offer grounded in the oneness of God stands directly behind this passage. The verbal and theological overlap is strong.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.
echoes.note: 'There is one God' restates the Shema's confession that the LORD is one, the foundational monotheistic creed of Israel. Paul reframes the Shema christologically by adding the one mediator, but the bedrock affirmation of divine oneness is directly drawn from Deuteronomy. This is the clearest scriptural anchor of verse 5.

echoes.text: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand. After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall […]
echoes.note: The Servant who makes his life an offering for sin and bears the sin of many provides the scriptural template for Christ giving himself as a ransom for all. The substitutionary self-offering 'for many' is universalized by Paul to 'for all.' The Servant Song is a primary source for the ransom theology of verse 6.

echoes.text: that they may offer sacrifices of pleasant aroma to the God of heaven, and pray for the life of the king, and of his sons.
echoes.note: The Persian decree provides for sacrifices and prayers 'for the life of the king and his sons,' a precedent for the synagogue practice of intercession for the ruling power that Paul commends to the church. This institutionalized prayer for the Gentile monarch stands behind the apostolic instruction. The continuity of Jewish intercession for kings informs the exhortation.

echoes.text: and pray for the life of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon, and for the life of Baltasar his son, that their days may be as the days of heaven above the earth: and the Lord will give us strength, and lighten our eyes, and we shall live under the shadow of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon, and under the shadow of Baltasar his son, and we shall serve them many days, and find favor in their sight.
echoes.note: Baruch directs prayer for the life of Nebuchadnezzar and his son Belshazzar, that the exiles may live under their shadow and find favor, mirroring the petition for kings so believers can live quietly. The deuterocanonical text models the very practice of interceding for a foreign sovereign's reign for the sake of the people's peace. It is a close conceptual parallel to verses 1-2.

echoes.text: Tell them, As I live, says the Lord Yahweh, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn, turn from your evil ways; for why will you die, house of Israel?
echoes.note: The oath 'As I live, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live' restates the divine saving desire that Paul invokes in saying God wills all people to be saved. The emphatic divine self-witness to a will for repentance and life parallels Paul's theology of God our Savior. It complements the Ezekiel 18 echo.

echoes.text: There is no umpire between us, that might lay his hand on us both.
echoes.note: Job's lament that 'there is no umpire between us, who might lay his hand on us both' articulates the need for a mediator between God and man that Paul declares fulfilled in the one mediator Christ Jesus. The longing for an arbitrator standing between God and humanity is answered in verse 5. The conceptual correspondence to 'one mediator' is notable though not verbal quotation.

echoes.text: On the next day, Moses said to the people, “You have sinned a great sin. Now I will go up to Yahweh. Perhaps I shall make atonement for your sin.” Moses returned to Yahweh, and said, “Oh, this people have sinned a great sin, and have made themselves gods of gold. Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.”
echoes.note: Moses standing between the LORD and the people, offering himself to make atonement for their sin, typifies the role of the one mediator that Paul ascribes to Christ. The Mosaic mediation at Sinai is the paradigmatic Old Testament instance of a man interceding between God and men. Christ as mediator is read against this figural background.

echoes.text: “When you take a census of the children of Israel, according to those who are numbered among them, then each man shall give a ransom for his soul to Yahweh, when you number them; that there be no plague among them when you number them.
echoes.note: The atonement money, a ransom for each life given at the census so that no plague befall them, supplies the cultic background for Christ giving himself as 'a ransom for all.' The Hebrew kopher / lytron concept of a redemptive price for life stands behind Paul's ransom language. The universalizing 'for all' extends the Exodus ransom to all humanity.

echoes.text: The king’s heart is in Yahweh’s hand like the watercourses. He turns it wherever he desires.
echoes.note: The conviction that the king's heart is a watercourse in the LORD's hand, turned wherever he wills, undergirds the rationale for praying for rulers: God can move them toward conditions of peace. Paul's confidence that prayer for kings yields a tranquil life presupposes divine sovereignty over rulers. The link is thematic rather than verbal and is faint.

echoes.text: Don’t we all have one father? Hasn’t one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, profaning the covenant of our fathers?
echoes.note: 'Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us?' offers a parallel monotheistic confession linked to the unity of humanity, resonant with Paul's 'one God' grounding the universality of salvation. The pairing of divine oneness with the common bond of all people overlaps with the passage. The connection is thematic and secondary to the Shema.

echoes.text: (I stood between Yahweh and you at that time, to show you Yahweh’s word: for you were afraid because of the fire, and didn’t go up onto the mountain;) saying,
echoes.note: Moses' statement that he stood between the LORD and the people to declare the word, because they feared the fire, presents him as mediator of the covenant, prefiguring the one mediator language. The Mosaic mediatorial office informs Paul's category. The link is figural and faint.

echoes.text: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough,
echoes.note: The psalm's note that no one can by any means ransom another or give to God a price for his life sets up, by contrast, the ransom that Christ alone provides 'for all.' Paul's ransom claim answers the human impossibility the psalm laments. The link is conceptual and contrastive.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest. How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you arise out of your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: so your poverty will come as a robber, and your scarcity as an armed man.
echoes.note: The manager's frantic foresight against future destitution ('I have no strength to dig, I am ashamed to beg') inverts the sluggard wisdom of Proverbs, where prudent provision against want is praised. The shared topos of provident foresight versus ruinous idleness gives modest coherence, though no verbal contact; faint and contested.

echoes.text: There was no bread in all the land; for the famine was very severe, so that the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan fainted by reason of the famine. Joseph gathered up all the money that was found in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, for the grain which they bought: and Joseph brought the money into Pharaoh’s house. When the money was all spent in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph, and said, “Give […]
echoes.note: Joseph as the shrewd steward managing his lord's grain and debtors during scarcity offers a figural backdrop to a manager renegotiating debts of wheat and oil. Coherence is thematic (estate-steward over produce), but the moral valence is opposite and there is no diction overlap, so it is faint and contested.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Make friends by means of unrighteous mammon, so that they may receive you into the eternal tents' coheres tightly with the proverb that lending to the poor lends to the LORD, who repays. The shared logic that present generosity with money secures future, divine reception gives strong coherence with a widely available sapiential maxim.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's counsel that almsgiving 'lays up a good treasure against the day of necessity' and 'delivers from death' supplies the precise economy Jesus assumes: wealth converted into mercy yields eschatological security. High coherence and Second-Temple availability make this a strong deuterocanonical echo behind 'receive you into the eternal tents.'

echoes.text: Howbeit with a man in poor estate be longsuffering; And let him not wait for your alms. Help a poor man for the commandment’s sake; And according to his need send him not empty away. Lose your money for a brother and a friend; And let it not rust under the stone to be lost. Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold. Shut up alms in your store-chambers; And it shall deliver you out of all […]
echoes.note: Ben Sira urges laying up alms in one's treasury as a deposit that will rescue one from misfortune, framing charity to the poor as deferred self-interest. The volume and coherence with 'make friends... so they may receive you' is high, and Sirach was demonstrably available to Luke's milieu.

echoes.text: Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor; if there may be a lengthening of your tranquility.
echoes.note: Daniel's appeal to Nebuchadnezzar to 'redeem your sins by almsgiving and your iniquities by mercy to the poor' supplies the redemptive-almsgiving theology underlying using mammon to gain eternal welcome. Strong coherence with the verse's logic; the connection is conceptual rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Incline your ear to a poor man, And answer him with peaceful words in meekness. Deliver him that is wronged from the hand of him that wrongeth him; And be not faint-hearted in giving judgement. Be as a father to the fatherless, And instead of a husband to their mother: So will you be as a son of the Most High, And he will love you more than your mother does.
echoes.note: The maxim 'faithful in a very little is faithful in much' coheres with Ben Sira's wisdom that integrity in small dealings with the lowly proves character, but the gnomic form is broadly diffused and no single passage controls it. Faint and contested as a specific source.

echoes.text: If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose this day whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.”
echoes.note: 'No servant can serve two masters... you cannot serve God and Mammon' echoes the covenantal either/or of choosing whom to serve, the LORD versus rival gods. Coherence with the exclusive-service motif is real but the diction is independent, so it is a faint figural echo at best.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The demand for undivided love of God set against love of money draws on the Shema's totalizing claim ('with all your heart'), which forbids a divided heart. The opposition of single-hearted devotion versus a rival master gives modest coherence; verbal contact is absent, so it is contested.
